title: Contingent valuation

definition.text: A survey-based technique for putting a money value on things that are not sold in markets, such as a protected environment or the harm done by pollution.

facts.text: The survey usually asks how much people would pay to keep an environmental feature such as biodiversity, or how much they would need to be paid to accept its loss.
It is called a stated preference method, as opposed to revealed preference methods that rely on prices people actually pay.
Ciriacy-Wantrup proposed the idea in theory in 1947, and Robert K. Davis first applied it in 1963 to value a wilderness area for hunters and tourists.
It rose to prominence in the United States in the 1980s, when governments gained authority to sue for damage to environmental resources held in trust for the public, including non-use values.
The Exxon Valdez oil spill was the first case where its surveys were used to put numbers on damages.
Critics warn of strategic answers, protest answers, response bias and respondents ignoring their income limits, and many economists prefer evidence from real market purchases.
US government departments have used it widely in cost-benefit analyses of projects that affect the environment, such as valuing river recreation below Glen Canyon dam.
Clive Spash's research found that many willingness-to-pay answers behaved like charitable donations rather than the trade prices economists assumed.

contested_note: Many economists doubt that survey answers about willingness to pay reflect real values, while defenders say newer survey designs have fixed the early biases.

definition.text: A panel of leading economists, chaired by Kenneth Arrow and Robert Solow, convened by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to judge whether contingent valuation surveys could be trusted.

facts.text: It heard 22 expert economists and published its results in 1993.
It recommended personal interviews, a yes-or-no referendum format on a specific tax, and detailed information about the resource and its threats.
Preferring cautious estimates, it advised measuring willingness to pay to protect a good rather than willingness to accept its loss.
It judged that well-designed surveys were reliable enough to start a legal damage assessment, including passive-use values.

title: Ecosystem valuation

definition.text: The process of assigning a value, in money, physical units or other terms, to an ecosystem or the services it provides.

facts.text: Putting numbers on benefits such as a forest's flood control and carbon storage is meant to help policy-makers compare policies through cost-benefit analysis.
In 1997 Robert Costanza and colleagues made the first estimate of the worldwide worth of ecosystem services: $33 trillion a year.
It draws on stated preference methods such as contingent valuation and revealed preference methods such as hedonic pricing and travel cost.
TEEB found ecosystem service values ranging from roughly $100 per hectare per year for open ocean to more than $1,000,000 per hectare per year for the richest coral reefs.
Valuation is hard because many environmental goods, such as clean air, are not traded and may be non-rival and non-excludable.
Critics say preference-based valuation avoids deliberation and judgment, and the money value society gives to services depends on how income is distributed.
Some programmes go on to pay landowners for services; Costa Rica paid about $42 per hectare to preserve forests.

contested_note: Sources describe ecosystem valuation as philosophically and ethically controversial, with debate over whether nature should be priced at all.

definition.text: A revealed preference method that values a place without a market price, such as a national park or beach, from what visitors spend in time and money to get there.

facts.text: Harold Hotelling suggested it in a 1947 letter to the US National Park Service; Trice and Wood (1958) and Clawson (1959) refined it.
People living farther away spend more to visit and come less often, while those nearby visit more and spend less.
Visitors are grouped into distance zones, each zone's visit rate is regressed on travel cost, and the result builds a demand curve for the site.
The area under that demand curve gives willingness to pay for the site, used as its value in cost-benefit analysis.

definition.text: The smallest amount of money a person would take to sell a good or service, or to put up with a harm such as pollution.

facts.text: It is the counterpart of willingness to pay, the most a buyer would give up to get something or avoid something unwanted; both are reservation prices.
A trade's price falls between the buyer's willingness to pay and the seller's willingness to accept, and the gap between them is the economic surplus.
It can be estimated with choice experiments or asked directly in contingent valuation surveys.
Formally, it is the payment that makes a person's utility after an unwanted change, with compensation, equal to their utility before it.
Which measure applies depends on property rights: if lakeside residents have a right to a clean lake, their willingness to accept compensation for pollution counts.

title: WTA–WTP gap
article: Willingness to accept#Standard theory versus experimental results

definition.text: The finding that people ask far more to give something up than they would pay to get it, even though standard theory predicts the two amounts should match.

facts.text: Ziv Carmon and Dan Ariely found willingness to accept for basketball tickets was more than 10 times willingness to pay.
Explanations include income limits on what people can pay and the endowment effect, where owning something triggers loss aversion.
Plott and Zeiler argued the gaps partly reflect participants misunderstanding the experimental task.
The gap matters for contingent valuation, where endowment effects are widespread.

contested_note: Researchers disagree whether the gap reflects real loss aversion or flaws in experimental design.
notes: Endowment effect page gives 14 times for the Carmon and Ariely tickets (S:7d48828611ef), compatible with 'more than 10 times'.

title: Choice modelling

definition.text: A family of methods that model how a person or group decides, using either their real choices or choices they state in a set context.

facts.text: It usually infers where items sit on a hidden scale, typically utility, from repeated choices of one option over another.
It is regarded as the best method for estimating willingness to pay for quality improvements that vary in several dimensions at once.
Its roots lie in Thurstone's 1920s research on food preferences and in random utility theory, which Daniel McFadden developed in economics.
McFadden used past transport choices to predict demand for the Bay Area Rapid Transit before it was built, work that earned him the 2000 Nobel economics prize.
A survey describes a good by attributes and levels; because full combinations explode, a phone with 2 brands, 3 shapes, 3 sizes and 4 memory options has 72, only a subset is shown.
It forces respondents to weigh trade-offs between attributes and lets analysts estimate implicit prices for each attribute.
In environmental economics, non-use values are usually estimated with stated preference methods such as contingent valuation or choice modelling.

notes: Terminology is disputed (choice-based conjoint vs discrete choice experiment) but this is naming, not a substantive debate.

definition.text: A revealed preference method that estimates the value of each characteristic of a good, such as a house, by breaking its price into contributions from its features.

facts.text: It is usually estimated with regression analysis and is used in real estate, environmental economics, marketing research and Consumer Price Index calculations.
In environmental work it measures how much a nearby amenity such as a park raises home prices, holding other house features fixed.
A house is treated as a bundle of features, such as bedrooms, lot size and distance from the city centre, each given its own price.
Hedonic modelling was first published in the 1920s to value farm land, with roots also traced to Court's 1939 study of car prices.
Some critics argue its use in the US CPI can understate inflation, while studies abroad show non-hedonic methods can misstate inflation by ignoring quality change.

title: Replacement cost

definition.text: The amount one would have to pay at today's prices to replace an asset with an undamaged equivalent.

facts.text: It can differ from market value and from 'actual cash value', which subtracts depreciation.
Insurers use it as one way to value an insured item, such as paying the price of a similar new television today.
In urban planning, the replacement cost of public infrastructure such as roads matters because it can push local governments toward bankruptcy.

notes: Page is insurance-focused and never mentions valuing ecosystems by replacement cost; the replacement cost method for ecosystem services is a gap.

title: Revealed preference

definition.text: A way of working out what people prefer from the choices they actually make, pioneered by Paul Samuelson in 1938.

facts.text: It assumes people's preferences show in their purchasing habits.
It arose because utility, the satisfaction behind choices, could not be measured directly, so economists defined it from observed behaviour instead.
It contrasts with stated preference approaches, which ask people directly; economists usually trust revealed preferences more.
If bundle a is chosen when bundle b was also affordable, a is said to be revealed preferred to b.
In ecosystem valuation, revealed preference methods such as hedonic pricing and travel cost link a service to a market good to estimate willingness to pay.
Critics say a purchase cannot show which alternatives were given up, and that the theory wrongly assumes preferences stay constant over time.

contested_note: Several economists, including Amartya Sen and Stanley Wong, criticise the theory as tautological or a failed research programme.

title: Weak axiom of revealed preference
article: Revealed preference#The Weak Axiom of Revealed Preference (WARP)

definition.text: A consistency rule saying that if a consumer picks a over b when both are affordable, they will never pick b over a when both are affordable.

facts.text: The strong axiom (SARP) adds that choices cannot be indirectly revealed preferred to each other, which preserves transitivity.
The generalised axiom (GARP) extends SARP to cases where several bundles give equal utility, and rules out preference cycles.

definition.text: A 1967 result by Sydney Afriat proving that a finite set of observed choices satisfying GARP can be explained by a utility function.

facts.text: Its inequalities let the utility function be built directly from the data, unlike SARP, which only proves existence for infinite datasets.
It is widely used in econometrics to test rationality and build preferences from empirical data.

title: Compensating differential

definition.text: The extra pay a worker must be offered to take an unpleasant or risky job instead of other jobs they could do.

facts.text: For an especially pleasant job the differential is negative: workers accept lower pay.
The idea, credited to Adam Smith, has been used to study injury risk, the money value workers put on their own lives, and wage gaps between regions.
Economists usually expect wages to be lower in places with high levels of amenity, so wage gaps can reveal how much an area's attractiveness is worth.
A hedonic wage function plots how wages rise with a job's undesirable features, such as the probability of injury.

notes: Not the same as compensating variation (S:9fc5350430fd), which the page distinguishes.

definition.text: A survey-based statistical technique, mainly from market research, that works out how much people value each attribute that makes up a product or service.

facts.text: Respondents see a controlled set of products broken down by attribute, and their choices reveal the implicit value, or part-worth, of each attribute.
Marketing professor Paul E. Green developed it, and Jordan Louviere pioneered the choice-based version that underlies discrete choice analysis.
It is also called discrete choice modelling or stated preference research.
Because the number of attribute combinations grows exponentially, fractional factorial designs cut the profiles respondents must judge.

definition.text: Models that describe and predict choices between separate alternatives, such as which mode of transport to take, rather than how much of something to buy.

facts.text: A model gives the probability that a person chooses a given alternative as a function of features of the alternatives and of the person.
They can be derived from utility theory, and only differences in utility between alternatives affect the choice probabilities.
The first applications were in transportation planning, and in market research the approach is commonly called conjoint analysis.
Common forms include binary logit and probit, multinomial and conditional logit, nested logit and mixed logit, usually estimated by maximum likelihood.
Standard logit assumes independence of irrelevant alternatives, a substitution pattern that is not always realistic; mixed logit relaxes it by allowing tastes to vary between people.

definition.text: A bias in contingent valuation where people struggle to put a value on one public good that is part of a larger set of similar goods.

facts.text: It suggests contingent valuation is not an unbiased way to measure policy effects in cost-benefit analysis.
Part-whole bias arises when willingness to pay for two policies valued separately does not add up to willingness to pay for both together.
Willingness to pay for a project is larger when it is asked about first than when it comes second in a sequence.
One fix asks first what people would pay for the whole set of items, then how much of that should go to the named item.

title: Stated preference methods

definition.text: Valuation methods that measure what people value by asking them directly in surveys, rather than watching what they buy.

facts.text: Contingent valuation, which asks people their willingness to pay for an ecosystem or one of its services, is the best-known stated preference method.
Non-use values are usually estimated with stated preference methods such as contingent valuation or choice modelling, because people's market behaviour reveals nothing about them.
Ecosystem valuation divides its methods into stated preference and revealed preference families.
Conjoint analysis and choice modelling are also used for stated preference research, and David Hensher and Jordan Louviere are credited with the first stated preference choice models.
Many economists distrust stated preferences and prefer people's revealed preferences in binding market transactions when judging willingness to pay.
Revealed and stated preference data can be combined to get the advantages of both.

contested_note: Many economists question whether survey answers can be trusted to measure willingness to pay.
notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own.

title: Benefit transfer

definition.text: A valuation method that estimates a project's benefits by borrowing the data, models and results of earlier studies of similar projects or sites.

facts.text: It comes in two forms: value transfer moves a single unit value from an earlier site, while function transfer uses valuation functions drawn from many studies and can be more accurate.
Meta-analysis can be used to build a valuation transfer.
Its common errors are measurement error, from biased study selection and assumptions, and transfer error, when the original and new sites do not correspond.
It is a cheap way to value a project when time and money rule out original research.

notes: Phrase concept; drafted on the Shadow price section that covers it.
